sources.content: The fate of the Lost Colony of Roanoke is one of America's most famous unsolved mysteries. Captains Phillip Amadas and Arthur Barlow returned with glowing reports of a "most pleasant and fertile" land, inhabited by a "loving and faithful" people, and it was decided that Roanoke Island's protected shores would be the perfect place to start England's first colony in the New World. As winter set in, food became scarce and tensions grew between the ill-prepared colonists and the Roanoke Islanders. These brave new colonists (two of them pregnant!) arrived at Roanoke in July of 1587. The colonists were left on Roanoke to settle in the abandoned ruins of their predecessors. White would make several more attempts to find his family and friends, but the fate of the Lost Colony of Roanoke remains a mystery to this day. sources.title: John White | Biography & Facts | Britannica
sources.content:
In May 1587 White sailed with more than 100 colonists as governor of a second colony that Sir Walter Raleigh attempted to found in North America. The colony was established on Roanoke Island that July, but on August 25, 1587, White returned to England. He arrived there in November, but, because of the approaching war with Spain, he was unable to secure a relief expedition immediately. When the expedition arrived at the island in August 1590, they found no trace of any colonists, including White’s daughter and his granddaughter, Virginia Dare. White retired to a home in Ireland. In February 1593 he wrote an account of his final voyage to Virginia.

In 1587, more than 100 English settlers came to Roanoke Island, commissioned by Queen Elizabeth I and led by Gov. John White, to establish a permanent settlement in the New World. Just three years later, when ships returned to bring supplies to the settlement, the island was deserted. There was no sign of the colonists except for the word “CROATOAN” carved into an abandoned structure and “CRO” etched into the bark of a tree.

sources.content: The fate of the Lost Colony of Roanoke is one of America's most famous unsolved mysteries. Captains Phillip Amadas and Arthur Barlow returned with glowing reports of a "most pleasant and fertile" land, inhabited by a "loving and faithful" people, and it was decided that Roanoke Island's protected shores would be the perfect place to start England's first colony in the New World. As winter set in, food became scarce and tensions grew between the ill-prepared colonists and the Roanoke Islanders. These brave new colonists (two of them pregnant!) arrived at Roanoke in July of 1587. The colonists were left on Roanoke to settle in the abandoned ruins of their predecessors. White would make several more attempts to find his family and friends, but the fate of the Lost Colony of Roanoke remains a mystery to this day. sources.content:
In May 1587 White sailed with more than 100 colonists as governor of a second colony that Sir Walter Raleigh attempted to found in North America. The colony was established on Roanoke Island that July, but on August 25, 1587, White returned to England. He arrived there in November, but, because of the approaching war with Spain, he was unable to secure a relief expedition immediately. When the expedition arrived at the island in August 1590, they found no trace of any colonists, including White’s daughter and his granddaughter, Virginia Dare. White retired to a home in Ireland. In February 1593 he wrote an account of his final voyage to Virginia.

In 1587, more than 100 English settlers came to Roanoke Island, commissioned by Queen Elizabeth I and led by Gov. John White, to establish a permanent settlement in the New World. Just three years later, when ships returned to bring supplies to the settlement, the island was deserted. There was no sign of the colonists except for the word “CROATOAN” carved into an abandoned structure and “CRO” etched into the bark of a tree.

Archaeologists recently uncovered a clue that doesn’t shed light on what happened to the lost colonists, but it may reveal more about their life on the island. sources.title: John White | Biography & Facts | Britannica
sources.content:
In May 1587 White sailed with more than 100 colonists as governor of a second colony that Sir Walter Raleigh attempted to found in North America. The colony was established on Roanoke Island that July, but on August 25, 1587, White returned to England. He arrived there in November, but, because of the approaching war with Spain, he was unable to secure a relief expedition immediately. When the expedition arrived at the island in August 1590, they found no trace of any colonists, including White’s daughter and his granddaughter, Virginia Dare. White retired to a home in Ireland. In February 1593 he wrote an account of his final voyage to Virginia.

# What Was the Lost Colony of Roanoke?

The Roanoke Colony was England’s first serious attempt to establish a permanent settlement in North America.

Governor John White led approximately 115 colonists to Roanoke Island in 1587.

Among them were:

Many popular stories exaggerate or distort the historical record.

### Myth: The colonists vanished overnight.

False.

The carefully dismantled settlement suggests a planned departure.

### Myth: Everyone was killed.

results.fact_check:
**CLAIM 1:** Lead poisoning was the decisive (primary) cause of the fall of the Western Roman Empire.  
**STATUS:** CONTRADICTED  
**EVIDENCE:** Both sources explain that lead poisoning was at most a minor health hazard and was not a single‑cause explanation for the empire’s collapse.  
**SOURCE URL:** https://www.unrv.com/articles/did-lead-poisoning-cause-the-fall-of-rome.php  

**CLAIM 2:** Lead concentrations in Roman wine/water reached up to **20 µg/g**, “far above safe limits.”  
**STATUS:** NEEDS SOURCE  
**EVIDENCE:** The supplied sources discuss high lead exposure and give qualitative statements (e.g., “250 mg daily for aristocrats”) but do not provide a specific measurement of 20 µg/g nor a direct safe‑limit comparison.  
**SOURCE URL:** https://www.unrv.com/articles/did-lead-poisoning-cause-the-fall-of-rome.php  

**CLAIM 3:** Existence of “Dr. Michele C. (University of Rome)” and the quoted statement attributed to him.  
**STATUS:** NEEDS SOURCE  
**EVIDENCE:** No mention of a Dr. Michele C. or any specific quotation appears in any of the supplied documents.  
**SOURCE URL:** https://www.unrv.com/articles/did-lead-poisoning-cause-the-fall-of-rome.php  

**CLAIM 4:** Lead leaches from the sweetened wine‑additive **sapa**, contributing to Roman lead exposure.  
**STATUS:** VERIFIED  
**EVIDENCE:** The academic PDF notes that “lead from sapa and wine containers contributed significantly to lead exposure among Romans.”  
**SOURCE URL:** https://www.academia.edu/122592045/Lead_poisoning_in_ancient_Rome  

**CLAIM 5:** “The true culprit was *something you eat*” – implying a definitive causal link between diet (lead‑tainted food/drink) and Rome’s collapse.  
**STATUS:** NEEDS SOURCE / UNVERIFIED (presented as fact without evidence)  
**EVIDENCE:** The sources treat lead poisoning as a hypothesis or minor factor, not a proven primary cause; no source confirms the phrasing as factual.  
**SOURCE URL:** https://www.unrv.com/articles/did-lead-poisoning-cause-the-fall-of-rome.php  

---

### OVERALL RESULT
- **Verified claims:** 1 (lead from sapa).  
- **Contradicted claims:** 1 (lead poisoning as primary cause of Rome’s fall).  
- **Claims needing revision or sourcing:** 4 (lead concentration figure, Dr. Michele C. attribution, diet‑culprit statement, and any absolute causality phrasing).

### CLAIMS NEEDING REVISION
1. Lead concentration figure “up to 20 µg/g – far above safe limits.”  
2. Attribution to “Dr. Michele C. (University of Rome).”  
3. Definitive wording that diet/lead was the *true culprit* behind Rome’s collapse
